title: Pasta con le Sarde
subtitle: Sicilian pasta with fresh sardines, fennel, raisins, and pine nuts
excerpt: Pasta con le sarde is one of Sicily's most celebrated dishes: pasta with fresh sardines, wild fennel, saffron, raisins, pine nuts, and toasted breadcrumbs. It is sweet, savoury, and aromatic all at once. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Pasta con le sarde is the emblematic dish of Sicilian cuisine, with roots in Arab-Norman cooking of the 9th to 12th centuries. The combination of fish with raisins, pine nuts, and saffron is characteristic of Arab culinary influence throughout the Mediterranean. The dish is associated with the feast of San Giuseppe (19 March) in some parts of Sicily, and is documented in Sicilian recipe collections from the 18th century onwards. Mary Taylor Simeti, Pomp and Sustenance (1989, Knopf), and Pino Correnti, Il libro d'oro della cucina e dei vini di Sicilia (1976, Mursia), both give detailed versions. The wild fennel (finocchio selvatico) is the authentic ingredient; cultivated fennel fronds are an acceptable substitute. The dish is classified as a Protected Designation under UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Sicily.

glossaryTerms.definition: The feathery green fronds of wild fennel, used extensively in Sicilian cooking. It has a more intense anise flavour than cultivated fennel. In the UK it grows on roadsides and clifftops; the fronds of cultivated fennel or fresh dill are substitutes. Do not confuse with fennel seeds, which have a different character.

content.text: Pasta con le sarde is an unusual pasta: it requires assembling multiple elements separately and combining them at the end, with toasted breadcrumbs scattered over the top in place of cheese. The sardines are sauteed with onion and saffron; the
is blanched and added to the sauce; the raisins and pine nuts provide the agrodolce character. The whole thing comes together with the pasta in the pan at the end.

Use fresh sardines, filleted and boned. Tinned sardines in oil are a very different ingredient and do not work here. Wild fennel fronds are the authentic ingredient; use the fronds from a cultivated fennel bulb, or a mixture of dill and fennel tops, as a substitute.

items.prepNote: wild or cultivated fennel fronds, roughly chopped
a generous pinch, steeped in 50ml hot water

content.text: Blanch the fennel and toast the breadcrumbs
Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Blanch {{fennel-fronds}} of fennel fronds for 2 minutes. Lift out with a slotted spoon and chop roughly. Reserve the cooking water to cook the pasta.
Toast {{breadcrumbs-coarse}} of breadcrumbs in 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crunchy. Set aside.

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large saute pan over medium heat. Add {{onion}} of onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft. Add {{anchovy-fillets}} of anchovies and stir until dissolved. Add the saffron with its soaking liquid, {{raisins}} of raisins, and {{pine-nuts}} of pine nuts.

Add the blanched fennel and stir to combine. Add {{sardines-fresh}} of fresh sardine fillets, breaking them into large pieces as they hit the pan. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the sardines are just cooked through. Season.

Cook {{pasta-dried}} of bucatini or spaghetti in the fennel-blanching water until al dente. Drain, reserving pasta water. Toss with the sauce, adding a splash of pasta water if needed. Serve immediately with the toasted breadcrumbs scattered over the top.

items.fix: Add sardines at the end and cook briefly. Fold gently; the fish should break into large pieces, not mush.

items.cause: Saffron not properly steeped, or raisin and pine nut quantities too low
items.fix: Steep the saffron in hot water for at least 10 minutes. The sweet-savoury-aromatic balance is the defining characteristic; use the full amounts.

content.text: Pasta con le sarde is the dish that best represents Sicilian culinary history. Its ingredients reflect nine centuries of Arab, Norman, and Greek influence on the island's cooking. The saffron and raisins came from the Arab-Norman kitchen; the sardines and fennel from the Greek and Roman tradition; the pine nuts from the Arab spice trade. In Palermo it is eaten on 19 March for the feast of San Giuseppe. Outside Sicily it is less common but entirely achievable. All the ingredients are available and the technique is simple once you understand how the elements fit together.
